avoid anything that could be stressful
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are strongly social-evaluative and interpersonal (avoiding evaluation, avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which contains no social threat, shame, or interpersonal trauma content to explain these strategies.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, the strongest pathway is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies. However, the selected negative appraisals focus on global identity change, chronic misery, and self-blame for being in the situation, while the selected strategies are specifically about managing social scrutiny and interpersonal interactions. That is a weak clinical fit: the strategies do not plausibly follow from the appraisals provided.

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Memory and appraisals are only partly coherent: terror on recall and olfactory recall fit disaster trauma, but rage on recall is less well supported by the rest of the profile because there is no accompanying appraisal about betrayal, preventability by others, or injustice that would explain intense anger as a central recall response.

For a natural-disaster trauma, intense rage specifically on recall is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on terror, misery, self-change, and generalized avoidance rather than anger at a person or agent. Rage can occur, but here it lacks support from the other selected items and is the least coherent memory item.

'Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation' implies preventable personal failure in getting into the trauma. With a natural disaster, this appraisal is difficult to justify unless there was a very specific risky decision context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other appraisals focus on post-trauma change and unhappiness, making this item the clearest mismatch.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, strong self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to justify clinically unless the disaster involved a very specific preventable action by the patient. In the absence of any such context, this appraisal is implausible for the indexed trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are predominantly interpersonal/social-safety behaviors (avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations) that fit social threat or shame-based trauma formulations more than a natural disaster PTSD presentation. They do not connect well to the memory/appraisal content provided.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile includes active hypervigilant threat-monitoring ('constantly scan environment for signs of threat') and a global danger appraisal, but the formulation specifies Threat as effectively inactive, with no active links involving Threat and no active Trigger pathways. For a natural-disaster case, these items imply an ongoing threat-focused maintenance pattern that is not supported by the stated formulation.

issues.item: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: This is not just a weak-edge issue: both items explicitly center current external danger/threat, whereas the active formulation is concentrated on Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory and Negative Appraisals ↔ Maladaptive Strategies without Threat involvement. The remaining items fit a self-focused/post-traumatic change formulation, making these threat-focused items the main incoherent elements.

vignette: Ethan was nineteen, a fresh-licensed fast-food crew member who had just started his first shift at the local diner after graduating high school. The day he was in the school gymnasium during a sudden tornado, a chain of rapid, crushing events unfolded. The ceiling above the gym cracked like a dry twig; wind howled like a freight train, and a piece of the roof collapsed onto the floor, sending a shower of dust and broken boards across the field of the gym. Ethan was on the third floor, in a classroom that had been used as a shelter, and the collapse sent him tumbling into a puddle of water and debris. He was pinned under a fallen locker, his chest pressed tight enough to choke him, and he could taste the bitter iron of blood in his mouth. When the tornado finally cleared, the air was thick with the scent of hot metal and wet concrete. He had spent twenty minutes trapped, feeling his body convulse and his heart hammer against his ribs, a terrifying memory that he could still feel in the present. The horror of that night had left Ethan with a bleak conviction that he was irrevocably changed. He had come to believe that the person he had become is unrecognisable to him, that his once-joyful laughter had been replaced by a constant gloom, and that the damage he sustained would forever shadow every corner of his life. These negative appraisals seeped into his daily routine, prompting him to rehearse what he would say before any conversation and to avoid any situation that might stir a stress reaction. Whenever he saw a co-worker's smile, he rehearsed a script of neutral words, certain that a slip would remind him of his failure to cope. Simultaneously, the negative appraisal that the event had left permanent scars sharpened the images that flooded his mind. When he was alone at night, he would relive the exact angle of the falling locker, the crackle of wind outside the gym walls, and the scent of hot concrete that lingers like a ghost. The terror on recall returned with the same intensity, while the smell of dust would seep into his thoughts at the slightest wind. In the same breath, his negative appraisal fed his memory, and his memory, in turn, intensified his negative appraisal, locking him into a cycle that seemed impossible to escape. At the diner, the hum of the refrigerator, the click of the cash register, and the hiss of the fryer all served as subtle triggers. Ethan would stand by the front counter during rush hour, listening to the clatter of silverware and the low murmur of customers, and feel a surge of dread as if a storm were approaching. In these moments, he suppressed thoughts about the disaster, forcing his mind to focus on the mundane task of flipping burgers. Yet the attempt to push away memories only made the images sharper; he could still see the cracked ceiling and smell the damp concrete. The suppression did not erase the terror; instead, each time he forced his mind away, the memory seemed to climb higher in his awareness. He had come to believe that he was a victim of a permanent change, and this belief fed his avoidance strategies. He avoided stepping into the parking lot during storms, refusing to drive at night, and often left his shifts early to stay indoors. The routine avoidance reinforced his conviction that the world was unsafe, that he could not trust the environment to keep him safe, and that his sense of self had been forever altered. For months, Ethan's avoidance grew more entrenched. He would rehearse conversations not just before interactions, but before every small decision-what to say to a customer, how to order a shift, how to explain a late arrival to his supervisor. Each rehearsal was a rehearsal of his perceived inadequacy; he felt the weight of every misstep as a testament to his brokenness. The rehearsal, in turn, deepened his negative appraisal: the more he believed he had failed, the more he convinced himself that he had lost his former happiness. When he could no longer find the motivation to finish a task, he would suppress the memories and instead immerse himself in the hum of the fryers, hoping the noise would drown out the echo of the storm. Yet each attempt to suppress only brought the images back with even more force, reinforcing his belief that his trauma had permanently damaged him. The day he finally reached out for help was after a particularly chaotic shift. A customer had a sudden flare of anger and began yelling at Ethan, who had rehearsed his response but felt suddenly unable to stay calm. The memory of the collapsing locker surged so forcefully that he felt his heart pound and his vision blur. He realized that his entire coping routine-his rehearsals, his avoidance, his suppression-was failing him in the very environment he worked. In that instant, the fear of losing control and the hope that someone could help him break the cycle became unbearable. He now seeks therapy with the aim of untangling his memory and re-gaining a sense of self that he once believed was lost forever. His most pressing fear is that he will never again feel the simple joy of a clean day at work, but he also hopes that, with help, he might learn to view the past as a part of him rather than a defining flaw.
